paragraphs: Hector answered, “Do not bring me wine, honored mother. It would unman me, and I would forget my strength. I dare not pour a drink offering to Zeus with unwashed hands, and a man spattered with blood and filth may not pray to the son of Cronus. Gather the matrons and go with offerings to the temple of Athena driver of the spoil. There, on the knees of Athena, lay the largest and finest robe in your house, the one you value most. Promise her also twelve yearling heifers that have never felt the goad, to be sacrificed in her temple, if the goddess will take pity on the town, on the wives and little children of the Trojans, and keep the son of Tydeus away from the good city of Ilium. He fights with fury and fills men’s souls with panic. So go to the temple of Athena, while I look for Paris and urge him on, if he will listen to what I say. I wish the earth would open her jaws and swallow him! Zeus bred him to be a curse on the Trojans, and on Priam and Priam’s sons. If I could only see him go down into the house of Hades, my heart would forget its heaviness.”

His mother went into the house and called her waiting-women, and they gathered the matrons from all over the city. Then she went down to her fragrant storeroom, where her embroidered robes were kept. These were the work of Sidonian women, whom Paris had brought over from Sidon when he sailed the seas on the voyage that carried off Helen. Hecuba took out the largest robe, the one most beautifully rich with embroidery, to give to Athena. It glittered like a star and lay at the very bottom of the chest. She set off with it, and many matrons went with her.

When they reached the temple of Athena, lovely Theano opened the doors. She was the daughter of Cisseus and the wife of Antenor, and the Trojans had made her priestess of Athena. The women raised their hands to the goddess with a loud cry. Theano took the robe and laid it on the knees of Athena, and as she did so she prayed to the daughter of great Zeus. “Holy Athena,” she cried, “protectress of our city, mighty goddess, break the spear of Diomedes and strike him down before the Scaean gates. Do this, and we will sacrifice twelve heifers that have never known the goad in your temple, if you will have pity on the town, on the wives and little children of the Trojans.” So she prayed, but Pallas Athena did not grant her prayer.

While they were praying to the daughter of great Zeus, Hector went to the fine house of Paris. The foremost builders in the land had built it for him, with a house, storehouse, and courtyard near those of Priam and Hector on the acropolis. Hector went in, holding a spear eleven cubits long. Its bronze point gleamed ahead of him, fastened to the shaft by a ring of gold. He found Paris inside the house, busy with his armor, his shield and cuirass, and handling his curved bow. Argive Helen sat there too with her women, giving them their various tasks. When Hector saw Paris, he rebuked him with words of scorn. “Sir,” he said, “you do wrong to nurse this bitterness. The people are dying as they fight around this town of ours. You would blame anyone else you saw shirking his part in the fight. Up, then, or before long the city will be in flames.”

Paris answered, “Hector, your rebuke is fair, so listen, and believe me. I am not sitting here so much out of bitterness or ill will toward the Trojans as out of a wish to give way to my grief. My wife was just now gently urging me into battle, and I think it better that I go, for victory is always fickle. Wait while I put on my armor, or go ahead and I will follow. I am sure to catch up with you.”

Hector made no reply, but Helen tried to soothe him. “Brother,” she said, “I am a loathsome, sinful creature. I wish a whirlwind had caught me up on the day my mother gave birth to me and carried me off to some mountain, or into the waves of the roaring sea, to sweep me away before all this mischief came about. But since the gods have planned these evils, I wish at least that I had been wife to a better man, one who could feel the sting of dishonor and of men’s evil talk. This one has never been dependable, and never will be, and he will surely reap what he has sown. Still, brother, come in and rest on this seat. You are the one who bears the brunt of this toil, which was caused by my hateful self and by the sin of Paris. Zeus has doomed us both to be a theme of song among people yet to be born.”

Hector answered, “Do not ask me to sit, Helen, for all the goodwill you show me. I cannot stay. I am in a hurry to help the Trojans, who miss me greatly when I am not among them. But urge your husband on, and let him hurry of his own accord to catch up with me before I am out of the city. I must go home to see my household, my wife and my little son. I do not know whether I will ever return to them, or whether the gods will make me fall at the hands of the Achaeans.”

Hector left Helen and soon reached his own house, but Andromache was not in it. She was out on the wall with her child and one of her maids, weeping bitterly. Finding her gone, he stopped on the threshold of the women’s rooms and called out, “Women, tell me the truth. Where has Andromache gone? Is she with my sisters, or with my brothers’ wives? Or is she at the temple of Athena, where the other women are appeasing the awful goddess?”

His good housekeeper answered, “Hector, since you ask me to tell you the truth: she did not go to your sisters or to your brothers’ wives, and she is not at the temple of Athena, where the other women are appeasing the awful goddess. She is on the high wall of Ilium. She had heard that the Trojans were being hard pressed and that the Achaeans were in great force, so she went to the wall in frenzied haste. The nurse went with her, carrying the child.”

When the housekeeper had finished speaking, Hector hurried from the house and went back down the streets the way he had come. He crossed the city and reached the Scaean gates, by which he would go out onto the plain. There his wife came running toward him. She was Andromache, daughter of great Eetion, who had ruled in Thebe under the wooded slopes of Mt. Placus and was king of the Cilicians. His daughter had married Hector, and now she came to meet him with a nurse who carried his little child in her bosom—a mere babe, Hector’s darling son, lovely as a star. Hector had named him Scamandrius, but the people called him Astyanax, because his father stood alone as chief guardian of Ilium. Hector smiled as he looked at the boy, but he did not speak. Andromache stood beside him weeping and took his hand in hers. “Dear husband,” she said, “your courage will be the death of you. Think of your infant son, and of my unhappy self, who before long will be your widow—for the Achaeans will fall on you all together and kill you. If I lose you, it would be better for me to lie dead and buried, because when you are gone I will have nothing left to comfort me except sorrow. I have neither father nor mother now. Achilles killed my father when he sacked Thebe, the good city of the Cilicians. He killed him, but out of shame he did not strip his body. He burned him in his wondrous armor and raised a barrow over his ashes, and the mountain nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, planted a grove of elms around his tomb. I had seven brothers in my father’s house, and all of them went into the house of Hades on a single day. Achilles killed them as they were with their sheep and cattle. My mother, who had been queen of all the land under Mt. Placus, he brought here with the spoil. He set her free for a great sum, but then the archer-queen Artemis took her in the house of your father. No, Hector—you who are father, mother, brother, and dear husband to me—have mercy on me. Stay here on this wall. Do not make your child fatherless and your wife a widow. As for the army, place them near the fig tree, where the city is easiest to scale and the wall is weakest. Three times their bravest men have come there and attacked it, under the two Ajaxes, Idomeneus, the sons of Atreus, and the brave son of Tydeus, either on their own initiative or because some soothsayer had told them to.”

Hector answered, “Wife, I have thought of all this too. But how could I face the Trojans, men or women, if I shirked the fighting like a coward? I cannot. I know nothing except how to fight bravely in the front ranks of the Trojan army and win glory for my father and myself. I know well that the day will surely come when mighty Ilium will be destroyed, with Priam and Priam’s people. Yet I do not grieve for any of them—not for Hecuba, or King Priam, or my many brave brothers who may fall in the dust before their enemies—as I grieve for you, on the day when one of the Achaeans robs you of your freedom forever and takes you away weeping. Perhaps you will have to work the loom in Argos at a mistress’s bidding, or carry water from the springs Messeis or Hypereia, brutally treated by some cruel taskmaster. Then someone who sees you weeping will say, ‘She was the wife of Hector, the bravest warrior among the Trojans in the war before Ilium.’ At that your tears will break out afresh for the man who would have kept that day of captivity from you. May I lie dead under the barrow heaped over my body before I hear your cry as they carry you into bondage.”

He stretched out his arms toward his child, but the boy cried and nestled against his nurse’s bosom. He was scared by the sight of his father’s armor and by the horsehair plume nodding fiercely from the helmet. His father and mother laughed at him. Hector took the helmet off his head and laid it gleaming on the ground. Then he took his darling child, kissed him, and dandled him in his arms, praying over him to Zeus and to all the gods. “Zeus,” he cried, “grant that this child of mine may be like me, chief among the Trojans. Let him be just as excellent in strength, and let him rule Ilium with his might. Then may someone say of him as he comes home from battle, ‘The son is far better than the father.’ May he bring back the blood-stained spoils of the man he has laid low, and let his mother’s heart be glad.”

With this he put the child back in the arms of his wife, who took him to her own soft bosom, smiling through her tears. Her husband watched her, and his heart went out to her. He caressed her fondly and said, “My own wife, do not take these things so bitterly to heart. No one can send me down to Hades before my time. But once a man has been born, whether he is brave or a coward, there is no escape for him when his hour has come. Now go inside the house and busy yourself with your daily duties, your loom, your distaff, and the ordering of your servants. War is the business of men, and mine above all others born in Ilium.”

He picked his plumed helmet up from the ground, and his wife went back to her house, weeping bitterly and often looking back at him. When she got home she found her maidens inside and told them all to join in her lament. So they mourned Hector in his own house although he was still alive. They believed they would never see him return safe from the battle and from the furious hands of the Achaeans.

Paris did not stay long in his house. He put on his fine armor overlaid with bronze and hurried through the city as fast as his feet could carry him. As a stabled, well-fed horse breaks loose and gallops proudly over the plain to the place where he is used to bathing in the fair-flowing river—he holds his head high, his mane streams over his shoulders, and he exults in his strength and flies like the wind to the haunts and feeding ground of the mares—in the same way Paris went out from high Pergamus, gleaming like sunlight in his armor, and he laughed aloud as he sped swiftly along. Soon he came upon his brother Hector, who was just turning away from the place where he had talked with his wife. Paris spoke first. “Sir,” he said, “I am afraid I have kept you waiting when you are in a hurry, and I did not come as quickly as you told me to.”

“My good brother,” Hector answered, “you fight bravely, and no one with any fairness can belittle what you do in battle. But you are careless and willfully slack. It grieves me to the heart to hear the bad things the Trojans say about you, for they have suffered much on your account. Let us go. We will put things right later, if Zeus grants that we set the cup of deliverance before the ever-living gods of heaven in our own homes, once we have chased the Achaeans from Troy.”
